title: Manual handling
siteNotes: Where trolleys, sack trucks, keg lifts, hoists and other handling aids are kept
The venue's own arrangements for moving kegs and gas, and who is allowed to do it
Laundry arrangements (bag sizes, trolleys, stairs) and luggage trolleys
Who to ask for help on each shift
Any venue weight guidance, if the manager has set one
legalNotes: Avoid hazardous manual handling where reasonably practicable, assess what cannot be avoided, and reduce the risk: Manual Handling Operations Regulations 1992, reg. 4. https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/1992/2793 and https://www.hse.gov.uk/msd/manual-handling/index.htm (the avoid, assess, reduce approach was checked on the HSE page).
The law does not set specific weight limits: HSE manual handling overview (checked).
Factors to consider: task, individual, load and environment (TILE): HSE INDG143 'Manual handling at work: a brief guide', https://www.hse.gov.uk/pubns/indg143.pdf (checked).
Employees must make full and proper use of any system of work or handling aids provided: Manual Handling Operations Regulations 1992, reg. 5. Not checked against the text in this session.
Team lifting is not automatically safer; it needs planning and communication: HSE INDG143 (checked).
Good technique (load close, stable posture, avoid twisting, bend the knees) is HSE INDG143; HSE stresses technique does not make a very heavy load safe (checked).

No weight figures are given in the slides because the law sets none and the HSE overview page did not state any. HSE has published guideline figures elsewhere; they were not verified here and were deliberately left out.
Training on induction: Management of Health and Safety at Work Regulations 1999, reg. 13.

Review Oct 2026: checked, no changes. Reg. 4 is 'so far as is reasonably practicable'; the slides say 'where practicable' in plain words, which is acceptable. The law sets no weight limit; the HSE guideline figures in INDG143 are deliberately not quoted.

cards.title: Manual handling
cards.body:
By the end of this session you can:
- size up a lift before you do it
- use aids and teamwork when needed
- say no, or ask for help, when a load is not safe

cards.title: Most injuries are slow-burn
cards.body:
Back and shoulder injuries often build up from lots of small lifts, not one big one. In this job you carry kegs, laundry, trays, luggage and furniture all week.

> The law says to avoid hazardous lifting where practicable, assess what cannot be avoided, and reduce the risk. It does not set a weight limit.

items.title: Avoid
items.text: Can the lift be avoided or done with a trolley?

items.title: Assess
items.text: If not, look at the task, you, the load and the space.

items.title: Reduce
items.text: Use aids, share it, or split the load.

cards.title: Size up the lift: TILE
cards.body: Before you lift, stop for a few seconds and run through four things.

items.title: Task
items.text: How far, how often, any twisting or reaching?

items.title: Individual
items.text: Are you fit, well, and able to manage it?

items.title: Load
items.text: Heavy, bulky, awkward, slippery or unstable?

items.title: Environment
items.text: Space, stairs, floor, light and temperature?

cards.title: Make the job easier
cards.body:
The best lift is the one you do not do. Use a trolley, sack truck, keg lift or hoist if there is one. Break loads into smaller ones, plan your route and clear it first.

> Your manager will show you what aids the venue has and where they are kept.

items.title: Good technique
items.text: Load close, steady feet, no twisting.

items.title: Share the load
items.text: A planned team lift, or smaller loads.

items.title: Use an aid
items.text: Trolley, sack truck, lift or hoist.

items.title: Avoid the lift
items.text: Can it be moved another way, or not at all?

cards.title: Kegs, laundry, trays and luggage
cards.body: Each has its own trap. Kegs are heavy and awkward on cellar steps. Wet laundry is heavier than it looks. A tray held away from the body strains the shoulder. Luggage can be heavy and unbalanced.

items.title: Kegs
items.text: Use the aids provided. Ask for help on steps.

items.title: Laundry
items.text: Do not overfill bags. Use a trolley.

items.title: Trays
items.text: Keep loads balanced and close to your body.

items.title: Luggage
items.text: Use a trolley. Ask a guest if a bag feels very heavy.

cards.title: Lift with a plan
cards.body: Technique helps, but it does not make a very heavy load safe.

items.title: Lift smoothly
items.text: Bend the knees, keep your back steady.

items.title: Move, no twisting
items.text: Turn with your feet, set down carefully.

cards.title: Lifting with someone else
cards.body: Two people are not always safer. A team lift needs a plan: agree who leads, who counts, where it is going, and when to put it down. If one person is much taller, or you are not in step, the load can swing.

left.title: Do
items: Agree a plan and a signal

cards.title: When to say no
cards.body: It is fine to say a load is too heavy, awkward or unsafe for you. Do not lift if you are injured, unwell or unsure. Ask for help, a different method or an aid. Tell your manager if a task keeps being a struggle.

cards.title: Remember
cards.body:
- Stop and think: task, individual, load, environment
- Avoid the lift if you can; use a trolley or aid
- Keep the load close and do not twist
- Plan team lifts and agree a signal
- It is fine to say no, or ask for help

cards.q: You need to move a full keg from the delivery area to the cellar down steps. What is best?
options: Use the venue's aids or ask for help, and clear the route
Carry it quickly to get it over and done with
Roll it down the steps to save lifting it
Ask a guest to hold the door while you lift it
cards.why: Avoid or reduce hazardous lifts by using aids and help, particularly on steps. Your manager will show you the venue's way of doing this.

cards.q: If two people lift a load together, it is always safe.
cards.why: A team lift needs planning and communication. Poor coordination can make it more dangerous.

cards.q: Which TWO are part of assessing a lift using TILE?
options: The environment (space, floor, stairs)
How much the item costs
The load (weight, size, grip)
How many guests are watching
Whether the item is new
cards.why: TILE is task, individual, load and environment.

cards.q: Your back is sore and a colleague asks you to help lift a heavy linen bag. What do you do?
options: Lift it anyway to avoid making a fuss
Say you are not fit to lift and suggest a trolley
Drag it along the corridor instead of lifting
Lift it quickly before the pain gets any worse
cards.why: The individual is part of the assessment. If you are injured or unwell, say so and use another method.

cards.q: What does the law say about weight limits for manual handling?
options: Nothing may ever exceed 10 kg for any task
Staff can lift anything if they use good technique
No set weight limits exist, so each lift is assessed
Only men are allowed to lift heavy loads
cards.why: The law sets no fixed limits. Assess the task, the individual, the load and the environment each time.

cards.q: You should keep a heavy bag at arm's length so it is away from your body.
cards.why: Keep loads close to the body; holding them away puts more strain on your back and shoulders.

cards.q: Before lifting a crate of wine bottles, what should you do first?
options: Lift quickly before the load gets any heavier
Twist at the waist to save taking extra steps
Check the route is clear and you can grip the load
Ask a guest to give you a hand with it
cards.why: Stop and plan the lift: task, load, route and space.

cards.q: Two of you need to carry a heavy table through a doorway. What helps?
options: Agree who leads and a signal, and clear the route
Both lift at once and see what happens
Let the taller person take it alone
Drag it on its legs
cards.why: A team lift needs a plan and clear communication.

cards.q: If a trolley is available for the laundry, you should still carry the bags by hand to save time.
cards.why: Use the aid provided. Avoiding the lift is the first choice.

cards.q: A guest asks you to carry a very heavy suitcase up two flights, and you are not sure you can manage. What do you do?
options: Carry it in short bursts, resting on each landing
Carry it on your shoulder to save your arms
Tell the guest to leave it in reception for good
Say it is too heavy alone and use a trolley or help
cards.why: It is fine to say no, and to use an aid or ask for help.
